drainage.local_h: Why a flat Hallsville backyard holds water
local: A lot of Hallsville homes sit on a graded pad. The builder cuts and fills the lot flat, sets the slab and lays sod over the top. Then the fill settles. A year or two later the backyard has a shallow dish in it that holds water for a day after a hard rain. Nothing is broken. The ground simply has no fall. That is the first thing we check on a newer Hallsville lot, along with where the downspouts empty.

The soil adds to it. High ground around here tends to be sandy loam that soaks up water quickly. Low spots sit on heavier clay that does not. When a flat yard has both, rain sinks in on the high side and creeps into the clay on the low side, where it sits. The same yard can look fine in a drizzle and flood after a storm. Seeing it during or right after a rain tells us more than any tape measure.

Most of these yards do not need a French drain first. Regrading to give the ground fall, about six inches over the first ten feet, a swale that carries water across the lot and a pop-up emitter at the end of it fix many Hallsville backyards. Roof water is the other big one. Downspouts that dump against the slab get solid pipe out to open ground. A French drain is for water trapped underground, and the estimate tells you if yours is.

The outlet decides everything. On a subdivision lot there is little room, so a swale has to end on your own ground and not at the neighbor's fence. On acreage out toward Harleton you may have a ditch or a low corner to run to, which can make the job simpler. Price follows pipe length, dig depth and where the water can leave. Small fixes run $450 to $1,000, and a single French drain run is $1,900 to $3,000.

faq.q: How much does it cost to fix standing water in a Hallsville yard?
faq.a: Most projects run $2,000 to $3,750. Small fixes like a downspout reroute or one low spot run $450 to $1,000, and a standard single French drain run is $1,900 to $3,000. Full systems run $3,000 to $4,500. Pipe length, dig depth and the outlet move the number, and you get it in writing.

faq.q: Why does my new-build backyard in Hallsville stay wet?
faq.a: Builders grade the lot flat, and the fill settles after the house goes up. That leaves low spots with no fall to carry water away. Roof runoff and a clay layer under the topsoil add to it. We walk the yard, find which of those is the cause and fix that one.

faq.q: Will regrading fix my yard, or do I need a drain?
faq.a: Often regrading is enough, sometimes with a swale and a pop-up emitter. We shape the ground so water falls away from the house, then check that it has somewhere to go. A French drain is for water trapped in the ground. If we think you need one, the written estimate says why.

faq.q: Can you drain my yard without tearing up the lawn?
faq.a: Usually most of it stays untouched. A downspout reroute or one regraded spot disturbs very little. A drain run means a trench, and we cap it with soil and sod or finish it in river rock. Dry weather makes the digging faster and cleaner, since wet clay is heavy and sticky.

faq.q: My downspouts empty right beside the house. What can you do?
faq.a: We extend them in solid pipe out to open ground, or tie them to a pop-up emitter so the water leaves in a pipe and not across the yard. Small fixes like this run $450 to $1,000. We look at where the pipe can safely go before we quote it.

fertilization.local_h: A feeding plan for thin topsoil and tree line shade
local: Many newer Hallsville homes have builder sod laid over thin topsoil. The grass looks fine the first spring, then it runs hungry because there is little organic matter underneath to feed it. Builders also run heavy equipment over the lot, which packs the ground. That is why we pull a soil sample before we put anything down. The numbers tell us what the lawn lacks, and the written plan shows what goes down, when and why.

Sandy high ground and clay low spots need different handling. Sand lets nutrients wash through, so the high side of a lot wants steady, slow-release feeding and not one big dose. Clay holds nutrients but packs hard and drains slowly. Pine needles and acidic rain also push East Texas soil a little low on pH, so when the test says so, we add lime. Fertilizer works poorly when the pH is off.

Our dates follow the soil, not the store shelf. The first feeding goes down around the end of April, once nights stay above 60 degrees. Soil in Gregg and Harrison counties does not reach 65 degrees until mid-April, so feeding in March mostly washes out with the next rain. A lighter summer feeding goes down in early July, the last real nitrogen in early September and a potassium-heavy winterizer in late October.

Shade changes the plan along the tree lines. St. Augustine near the pines and hardwoods at the back of a lot grows slower, and late nitrogen on damp turf feeds large patch, which is why October is a potassium month. Compacted clay lawns get core aeration between late August and mid-September, with the feeding right behind it. We coordinate every visit with your mowing schedule so the lawn is cut and fed in the right order.

faq.q: How much does lawn fertilization cost in Hallsville?
faq.a: Visits start from about $190. A full program is four visits, and the price depends on your lawn size, the number of rounds, the grass type and whether the soil test calls for lime or you add core aeration. You get the plan and the price in writing before the first application.

faq.q: Why did my builder sod stop looking good after a year or two?
faq.a: Builder sod is often laid over thin topsoil on a packed base, which gives roots little to work with. The grass uses up what is in the soil and then runs hungry. A soil test shows what is missing, and a slow-release schedule plus aeration where the ground is packed helps it recover.

faq.q: When should the first fertilizer go down on a Hallsville lawn?
faq.a: Around April 25, once overnight lows stay above 60 degrees and the grass is fully awake. Earlier than that, bermuda and St. Augustine are half dormant and cannot pull it in, so much of it washes out in the next rain. The last real nitrogen goes down in the first two weeks of September.

faq.q: Do you test the soil and add lime?
faq.a: Yes. We pull a sample before the plan is written, and if the pH has drifted low we correct it with lime. Pine needles and acidic rain do that to a lot of East Texas yards. Fertilizer on soil with the wrong pH does less than it should.

faq.q: Should I aerate a lawn on clay?
faq.a: If it is compacted, yes. Construction traffic packs new-build lots, and clay holds that compaction. We core aerate between late August and mid-September and put the feeding right behind it. Aeration lets water, air and fertilizer reach the roots instead of running off.

flower-bed-installation.local_h: Beds built for Hallsville heat, clay and tree line shade
local: The front bed on a newer Hallsville house is usually a builder's row: a few shrubs in a line against the brick and a strip of mulch. We start by changing the shape. A deeper bed with a clean cut edge looks like it belongs to the house, and it gives the plants room to fill in. Then comes the part nobody sees. Roots get pulled, the soil gets turned and compost goes into the top few inches.

Plants follow the light. In full sun along the front of a south or west facing house we use knockout roses, salvia, lantana, dwarf yaupon and plumbago, all of which take East Texas heat. Hydrangeas and azaleas go where they get afternoon shade, such as the east side of a house or the edge of a tree line. Petunias and impatiens look great in April and are gone by the Fourth of July, so we skip them.

Drainage decides where a bed lives. Many flat Hallsville yards hold water at the low, clay end, and most of these plants hate wet feet. On those spots we raise the bed a few inches and set the grade so water moves off. On the sandy high ground the opposite problem shows up, and compost helps the soil hold moisture. Either way we tell you to water deep and less often, because daily watering in clay kills good plants.

Pine needles and leaves from the tree line land in these beds every fall, so we plan for it. Mulch goes down at an inch to an inch and a half, pulled back off the stems. If you want to see the layout first, the $199 Flower Bed Preview gives you a rendering. Shrubs and perennials plant best from September through November, and heat lovers like vinca wait for warm soil in mid-May and later.

faq.q: What plants hold up in full sun on a Hallsville lot?

faq.q: My builder bed keeps dying. What is going wrong?
faq.a: Usually the soil, not the plants. Builder beds often have compacted clay, a thin layer of mulch and shrubs planted too close together. We pull the bed apart, loosen and amend the soil, reset the grade and replant with real spacing so air moves through the plants.

faq.q: Do you put landscape fabric under the mulch?

faq.q: When is the best time to plant a bed in Hallsville?
faq.a: Fall, September through November, for shrubs and perennials, while the soil is warm and the air cools. Heat lovers like vinca should wait until the soil is truly warm, usually mid-May and later. Seasonal color rotates with the weather so the bed has something blooming most of the year.

Timing depends on the plant. Hollies and boxwoods get shaped in early summer, after the spring flush hardens off. Shade along the tree lines pulls hedges sideways. A shrub growing beside the pines at the back of a lot reaches for light and goes lopsided, and the needles and leaves that drop into it hang up in the branches. irrigation.local_h: Zoning a Hallsville yard for sand, clay and shade

Beds sit on spray instead of drip. Zones ignore where the shade falls, so grass in the open gets drowned while the strip under the pines stays dry. We repair what is broken, re-zone the system, or install a new one that fits the yard.

The soil changes inside one property. Higher ground is sandy and soaks water up fast, then dries out in July. Low spots sit on clay, which stops the water and holds it. One long cycle floods the low corner and leaves the high side thirsty. On a flat Hallsville pad, where water already struggles to move, shorter cycles that give it time to soak in work better than one long soak. We split zones by slope, sun and soil.

Beds go on drip. Spray heads in a bed wet the leaves, the mulch and the siding and still miss the roots. Drip puts water where the roots are and keeps foliage dry, which helps against the fungus that shows up in a wet, warm spring. Turf zones get heads spaced for full coverage. A system on city water gets a backflow prevention device, and new automatic systems get a rain or freeze sensor.

Texas treats irrigation as licensed work, so the design and install run under a Texas licensed irrigator, who checks every system. We run each zone and adjust it before we call the job done. Many East Texas cities require a permit and the rules vary, so we check what your address needs and pull it before we dig. Water source and pressure shape the design too. Send photos of the yard and of where your water line comes in.

We rework that into something that fits the house and holds up through July. We walk the property first and note where the sun falls, where the shade from the tree line reaches and where water goes after a storm. The plan comes from that, not from a catalog.

Grade comes before plants. On a flat graded pad we check that water moves away from the slab before anything gets mulched. If a low spot needs regrading or a downspout needs a pipe, it goes into the same job, which costs less than planting a bed and digging it up a year later. Retaining walls and drainage can be part of the same project where the site needs them.

Plants follow the ground. Sandy high spots dry out quickly and the clay low spots hold water, so one bed can need two different plant lists. Trees and shrubs go in with the root flare at grade and native soil back around them, never a pocket of bagged mix that turns into a bathtub in clay. In full sun we lean on lantana, salvia, plumbago, vinca and knockout roses, and we site azaleas and hydrangeas out of the worst afternoon sun.

Acreage works at a different scale. Out toward Harleton the job is usually a defined area near the house: beds, a shade tree, maybe a flagstone path. The rest of the property stays as it is. Fall is the best planting window, September to about Thanksgiving, because roots build for months before summer. To see the plan drawn first, the Landscape Design Preview is $199 for flower beds, $449 for hardscape and $999 for a full property, credited if you book within 90 days.

faq.q: How much does landscaping cost in Hallsville?
faq.a: Most projects run $900 to $3,600, and small bed refreshes start at a few hundred dollars. Large custom designs run more. The size of the area, plant count and size, mulch and edging materials, soil amendment or regrading, and add-ons like sod, walls or drainage all move the price.

faq.q: Can I see the plan before you dig?
faq.a: Yes. The paid Landscape Design Preview shows the plan first: $199 for flower beds, $449 for hardscape and $999 for a full property. The fee is credited toward the install if you book within 90 days. A simple refresh often goes straight to a written quote.

faq.q: Do you fix the grade as part of landscaping?
faq.a: Where the site needs it, yes. On flat Hallsville lots we check that water moves away from the slab, then regrade a low spot or add drainage in the same job. That way the new beds are not sitting in a puddle.

faq.q: What is the best time of year to plant in Hallsville?
faq.a: Fall, from September to about Thanksgiving. The soil stays warm while the air cools, so trees and shrubs build roots for months before summer heat. Spring works for summer color, but anything woody planted in April spends its first summer just trying to survive.

faq.q: Do you landscape acreage as well as subdivision lots?
faq.a: Yes. On acreage we usually focus on a defined area near the house and price it to the actual ground. Send your address and a few photos with the quote request, and we will walk it with you and put the plan and price in writing.

faq.q: Why is part of my Hallsville yard still wet days after rain?

leaf-removal.local_h: Why tree line lots in Hallsville need more than one pass
local: Tree lines on the back and sides of Hallsville lots do most of the dropping. Pecans go first, sweetgums let go in early November, and post oaks and water oaks hang on to dead leaves and shed a few at a time into February. One Saturday is rarely enough. Most lots need a pass in mid-November, another in mid-December and a last one before spring green-up, and a heavy canopy can need more.

Plenty of Hallsville lawns are part bermuda in the open and part St. Augustine in the shade of those same trees, and that matters. Bermuda goes dormant early, so leaves on it are mostly ugly. St. Augustine stays partly green into November and sometimes December, and a wet leaf mat over it sets up large patch. People find the dead circles in March and blame the cold. Treat leaves on a shaded St. Augustine strip as urgent.

Here is how a visit goes. The crew blows leaves out of the lawn, the shrub beds and the rock beds onto the street or another paved surface. We pull the leaf vacuum trailer up, vacuum them, shred them about 10 to 1 and haul them off. The hose reaches back into the yard for piles the trailer cannot get close to. On acreage lots where leaves come in off the woods behind the property, that reach saves a lot of hand hauling.

You get one flat price in writing before we start. It follows lot size, tree count, how deep the leaves are, the beds to clear and the number of passes. There are no bag fees and no hourly meter. We re-edge the bed lines the leaves buried and clear the drive, walks and patio. Exterior gutter clearing and post-storm cleanups are part of the service. Call in October if you can, and we will plan the passes around what your trees drop.

faq.q: How much does leaf removal cost in Hallsville?
faq.a: It is one flat price for the job, quoted in writing after a free walkthrough and before we start. Lot size, the number and type of trees, how deep the leaves are, the beds to clear, the number of passes and the distance to the street all play in. No bag fees and no hourly meter.

faq.q: How many cleanups does a Hallsville yard need?
faq.a: Most lots need three: mid-November, mid-December and one before spring green-up. Heavy canopy over St. Augustine can need weekly clearing for three or four weeks. Post oaks and water oaks keep dropping into February, so we time visits to what is actually falling on your lot.

faq.q: Can I just mulch the leaves into the lawn with the mower?
faq.a: Light early drops, yes. That is fine in October and it feeds the lawn. Once the heavy fall starts in November, a thick mat smothers the grass, and a wet mat over St. Augustine invites large patch. That is when a full cleanup beats mowing over it.

faq.q: Do you clear leaves out of shrub beds and gutters?
faq.a: Yes. Leaves are blown out of shrub beds and rock beds, and we re-edge the bed lines they buried. Exterior gutter clearing is part of the service, along with driveway, walk and patio clearing. Post-storm cleanups are covered too.

faq.q: What do you do with the leaves?

mulch-installation.local_h: Mulching beds under Hallsville's tree lines
local: Mulch in Hallsville has a job beyond looks. Fall brings needles and leaves from the tree line into every bed, and by January a bed that was fresh in April looks tired. So we plan two windows. The big one is late April through mid-May, after the spring flush and before the heat. The second is late September through October, a thin top-dress that goes down before the leaves drop and the first cold front arrives.

Depth is where we part ways with the online calculators. They say three inches, a number from snow country. Three inches here sheds light rain like a tarp, holds moisture against stems and gives voles cover to eat roots through winter. We prep the bed and lay one to one and a half inches, pulled back off trunks and siding. For a 2,000 square foot bed, that is about 8 yards of mulch instead of 19.

Low clay spots are the other thing. A bed at the wet end of a flat Hallsville lot does not need more mulch piled on it. It needs the grade fixed so water leaves, and then a thin, even layer. Up on the sandy high ground, mulch is what holds moisture through July. And we never put landscape fabric underneath. Mulch is meant to turn into soil, and fabric stops that.

Shredded hardwood is what most beds get, and on a refresh we match what is already there. Pine straw is available, and it suits beds under the pines along many Hallsville lot lines. For bigger jobs we bring mulch in bulk by the yard, so you pay for mulch and not bags, and we use bagged mulch where access is tight. A fall top-dress over a layer still in place usually costs a fraction of a full install.

faq.q: How much does mulch installation cost in Hallsville?
faq.a: Most bed refreshes run $600 to $2,400. The price follows the square footage of the beds, how many beds, the type of mulch, how much edging and weed pulling they need, bulk delivery or bags, and whether it is a full install or a thin top-dress. A top-dress costs a fraction of a full job.

faq.q: How deep should mulch be?
faq.a: One to one and a half inches. That is deep enough to hold moisture and shade out weeds, and thin enough that rain reaches the roots. Three inches, which online calculators suggest, holds water against stems and gives voles cover. We pull mulch back from trunks and siding either way.

faq.q: Is pine straw or hardwood better for a Hallsville yard?
faq.a: Both work. Shredded hardwood is what most beds get, and it breaks down into better soil over about a year. Pine straw suits beds under pines and gives a lighter look. On a refresh we match what is already in the bed so it breaks down evenly.

faq.q: Should I put landscape fabric down first?
faq.a: No. Fabric stops mulch from turning into soil. We pull weeds by the root, loosen the top inch of soil so rain gets to the roots, and lay mulch directly at 1 to 1.5 inches. Mulch hides weeds, it does not kill them, which is why the pulling comes first.

faq.q: When is the best time to mulch?
faq.a: Late April through mid-May, after the spring flush and before the heat. A second, lighter pass in late September through October covers what the leaves and needles hide. If your beds are still covered but thin, the fall top-dress is usually all they need.

retaining-walls.local_h: Holding back a builder pad edge or a bank by a ditch
local: Hallsville is mostly flat, so a wall here usually answers a specific problem. A builder leaves a steep edge where the pad was cut or filled. A driveway cuts into a bank. Or the back of a lot drops toward a creek or ditch and the soil keeps washing out. Those are the spots where a wall earns its price. Before we quote one, we measure the drop and find where the water is coming from, because it is almost always the water that moves the dirt.

Every wall starts below grade. We dig out, compact a crushed stone base and set the first course dead level, since every course above inherits the bottom row. Behind the wall goes gravel backfill and a perforated drain carried out to daylight or a pop-up emitter. On clay, which swells when wet and shrinks when dry, that drain is what keeps pressure from building until the wall leans and bows.

Material depends on the job. We build with segmental block, natural stone, boulders and pressure-treated timber. Block suits a straight run along a driveway. Boulders and stone fit a bank by a ditch where a natural look matters. Taller walls get geogrid tied back into the hill and a slight lean into the slope, and if a wall is tall enough to need a stamped engineering plan, we tell you at the walkthrough.

Sometimes the answer is not a wall. A gentle slope can be handled by regrading and a planted bank, and we will say so after we walk it. If a wall is right, the price follows height, linear footage, material, excavation, drainage and engineering on tall walls. A short seating or garden wall starts at a few thousand dollars. We build year-round, and a dry stretch is best for digging, so do not wait on the spring rains if a slope is already washing out.

faq.q: How much does a retaining wall cost in Hallsville?
faq.a: Most walls run $3,000 to $19,000. Height and length move the number most. A short garden wall starts at a few thousand dollars, and tall structural walls run $20,000 and up. Material, excavation, drainage behind the wall and geogrid or engineering on taller walls also count.

faq.q: Do I need a wall, or will regrading do?
faq.a: On a gentle slope, regrading and a planted bank can do it. When you have to hold back a real drop, like a cut along a driveway or the edge of a pad, a wall makes sense. We measure the height and length and tell you which way we would go.

faq.q: What goes behind a retaining wall?
faq.a: Gravel backfill and a perforated drain pipe at the bottom, tied out to daylight or a pop-up emitter. That gives water a way out so it cannot build pressure against the wall. Taller walls also get geogrid tied back into the slope. It is the part you cannot see and the part that decides whether the wall lasts.

faq.q: Can you rebuild a wall that is leaning?
faq.a: Yes. Rebuilds of leaning or failed walls are part of the work. A wall usually leans because water has nowhere to go or the base was weak, so we fix the base and the drainage and rebuild it course by course. We tell you what we find when we walk it.

faq.q: Will a tall wall need an engineer?
faq.a: Some do. If a wall is tall enough to need a stamped engineering plan, we tell you at the walkthrough, before you commit, and it goes into the estimate. Height is what decides it, so we measure the drop first.

sod-installation.local_h: Sod prep on ground that runs from sand to clay
local: The first thing we check on a Hallsville yard is where it sits on the sand-to-clay range. High ground is sandy loam that drains fast. Low spots are heavier clay. That decides how much compost or topsoil goes in and how much leveling the ground needs. We till in two to three inches, then level and roll the bed so the sod lies flat. Sod laid over bare, packed fill is how new lawns fail.

Many Hallsville yards need new sod because of what the builder left: thin topsoil, builder sod that has gone patchy and a graded pad that holds water in the low spots. Before sod goes down in a low spot, we fix the water first, with a regrade or a swale, or the new grass sits in a puddle and rots. Dead turf and weeds are stripped to bare soil and hauled off.

Sun picks the grass. Bermuda needs six or more hours of direct sun, and it quits in shade. Along the tree lines, St. Augustine does better on four to six hours of dappled light. Plenty of Hallsville yards end up split, with bermuda in the open front yard and St. Augustine under the trees out back. For sun we usually lay Tif419 bermuda, and for shade Floratam, Palmetto or Raleigh. Under about four hours of sun no turf does well, and a bed is the better answer.

Timing and watering finish the job. Bermuda goes down best from late April through August and St. Augustine from May through September, and St. Augustine should be in by the end of September so it has four to six weeks of roots before dormancy. New sod needs a deep morning soak every day for two weeks, and we hand you a written schedule that tapers after that. Most projects run $1,500 to $4,700, by the pallet.

faq.q: How much does sod cost in Hallsville?
faq.a: Most projects run $1,500 to $4,700, priced by the pallet from the square footage you cover. A small patch repair costs less, and a large full-yard install with heavy prep costs more. Grass type, old turf removal, grading, soil amendment, drainage and pallet access all move the number.

faq.q: Bermuda or St. Augustine for my yard?
faq.a: Count the sun. Bermuda needs six or more hours of direct sun and holds up to kids and dogs. St. Augustine gets by on four to six hours of dappled light, like you get near a tree line. We read the yard in summer light and tell you which fits, or whether to split it.

faq.q: One corner of my Hallsville yard stays wet. Can you still sod it?
faq.a: Yes, after we fix the water. Sod on a low spot that holds water rots. We regrade or add a swale first so the corner drains, then amend and level the ground and lay the grass. Doing it in that order is cheaper than sodding twice.

faq.q: How long do I need to water new sod?
faq.a: A deep morning soak every day for the first two weeks, then a taper to deep, less frequent soaks once the roots take hold. Skip that in July heat and a new install can brown out in two weeks. We give you the schedule in writing.

faq.q: When can sod go down in Hallsville?
faq.a: Bermuda from late April through August. St. Augustine from May through September, finished by the end of the month so it roots before dormancy. Laid in November, St. Augustine just sits on the ground like a rug. Warm soil is what matters.

tree-planting.local_h: Shade for a bare Hallsville lot, planted to last
local: Newer Hallsville lots often come with a house, a slab and almost no shade. The usual ask is a tree that will cover the back patio someday. That is a good plan if the tree fits. We look at where the afternoon sun hits, how close the slab, the patio and the fence are, and how big the tree will get, then recommend species for that spot. Placement is half of it. A big tree set too near the house becomes a problem for the next owner.

Species follows the ground. For big shade we use live oak, post oak and southern magnolia. On the wetter, lower clay spots that a flat lot tends to have, red maple, river birch and bald cypress handle the water. On sandy high ground, trees dry out faster and need more watering in the first summers. We would usually plant a smaller tree that roots in fast over a big one that sulks, because a small fall-planted tree often passes the larger one.

Depth is where trees get killed. We set the root flare, where the trunk widens into its first roots, at grade or an inch above. In clay, a tree set too deep takes two or three years to die, so nobody blames planting day. The hole is two to three times as wide as the root ball and no deeper than the ball is tall. Native soil goes back in, because a pocket of bagged soil in clay holds water like a bathtub.

Fall is the best window, from September until around Thanksgiving, because the soil stays warm for weeks after the air cools. A tree planted in October gets close to six months of roots before summer. A container tree dries out fast in July, since it is drinking from its root ball and not your yard. We build a watering basin, lay a mulch ring off the trunk, stake only on windy sites and leave a written watering plan, with a 30-day check on bigger installs.

faq.q: How much does it cost to plant a tree in Hallsville?
faq.a: We do not publish a price, because the tree itself drives most of the cost. Species, size at planting, the number of trees, site access, the soil and drainage at the spot and staking all count. We walk the property, recommend a species and send a written quote that includes the aftercare plan.

faq.q: Which shade tree should I plant on a flat Hallsville lot?
faq.a: Live oak, post oak and southern magnolia give big shade. Red maple, river birch and bald cypress suit wetter, lower spots. We match the tree to its mature size and to how the spot drains before we plant. A tree set where water stands will struggle whatever the species.

faq.q: When is the best time to plant a tree here?
faq.a: Fall, September to about Thanksgiving. We plant year-round, but a spring tree gets only about eight weeks of roots before summer and needs more watering through its first July. A fall tree gets close to six months, so it goes into its first summer far better rooted.

faq.q: How often do I water a new tree?
faq.a: A new tree drinks from its root ball, so soak the ball with a hose on a trickle for about twenty minutes. For a fall tree, do that twice a week for six weeks, then weekly through November, then every ten to fourteen days in a dry winter. We leave the schedule in writing.

faq.q: How close to the house can you plant a shade tree?
faq.a: It depends on the tree's mature size. We look at the slab, the patio and the fence before choosing the species and the spot, and we would rather plant a smaller tree in the right place than a big one too close. We explain the choice at the walkthrough.

tree-shrub-care.local_h: Limbing up lot line trees and pruning on the right clock
local: On Hallsville acreage, the work is usually limbing up the pines and hardwoods that crowd the yard, clearing storm limbs and pulling out small volunteer trees that came up along fence lines. Dead lower branches shade the grass and hang over beds, so we cut those off shade trees and haul them away. Closer in, on subdivision lots, the work shifts to crepe myrtles, hollies and boxwoods that need the right cut at the right time of year.

Crepe myrtles are where we see the most damage. Topping them into stumps makes the tree grow back taller on weaker wood. We thin instead, taking out crossing and rubbing branches and limbing the tree up so the bark shows, in February while it is dormant. If a crepe myrtle has been topped for years, we plan the recovery over two or three winters and come back each dormant season to finish it.

Every plant has its own calendar. Knockout roses are cut back hard in February. Azaleas wait until right after they bloom. Hollies and boxwoods go in early summer. Oaks are left alone through spring and early summer, because the beetles that spread oak wilt go for fresh cuts, so we prune them in the dead of winter or the heat of late summer. Cuts go at the branch collar, sized to what the plant can close.

We remove small trees and shrubs that have died or outgrown their spot, clear storm damage and haul off every limb. We do not take down large trees close to a house, and we say so at the walkthrough if a job is bigger than what we handle. A pruning visit pairs well with a mulch refresh around tree bases and seasonal feeding for trees and shrubs. Pricing follows the number of plants, their size and condition, and the haul-off.

faq.q: How much does tree and shrub care cost in Hallsville?
faq.a: We do not publish a price, because the work varies too much. It depends on how many trees and shrubs you have, their size and condition, whether it is light shaping or recovery pruning, small removals and the debris to haul. You get a written, itemized quote after a free walkthrough, usually within a day.

faq.q: Will you clear small trees and brush along my fence line?
faq.a: We remove small trees and shrubs, prune limbs that hang over the yard and haul off storm debris. We do not take down large trees close to the house, and we tell you up front if a job is bigger than what we handle.

faq.q: When should I prune crepe myrtles?
faq.a: In February, while they are dormant and before the buds break. We thin them and do not top them. Topping makes the tree regrow taller on weaker wood. A tree that has been topped for years takes two or three winters to bring back.

faq.q: Why not prune my oak in spring?
faq.a: Oak wilt spreads partly through beetles drawn to the fresh sap of a pruning cut, and they are most active in spring and early summer. We prune oaks in the dead of winter or the heat of late summer, when the beetles are not drawn to fresh cuts.

faq.q: Can you clean up after a storm?
faq.a: Yes. Storm cleanup and limb haul-off are part of the service. We cut broken limbs clean, rake up the debris and haul it away. If a large tree is down or leaning on the house, that is a job for a tree service with the right equipment, and we say so.
